questions.question: What happens when you read a local variable that was declared but never assigned?
options: The code fails to compile
It reads as 0 for numeric types and null for references
It compiles but throws NullPointerException at runtime
It reads whatever value was left in that stack slot
questions.explanation: Unlike fields, local variables get no default value. The compiler performs definite-assignment analysis and rejects the program with a variable-might-not-have-been-initialized error. Fields DO default to 0, false or null, which is why the two are often confused.

questions.question: After running int x = 10; x = x++; what is the value of x?
options: It does not compile
questions.explanation: The post-increment evaluates to the OLD value 10 and then bumps x to 11 as a side effect. The assignment immediately writes the saved 10 back over it, so the increment is discarded. This is why x = x++ is a classic bug.

questions.question: One String is assigned from a literal and another is built with new String() from the same literal. What does comparing them with == give?
options: false, because new String() forces a separate object outside the pool
true, because both hold the same characters
true, because the compiler interns every String
It does not compile, because Strings cannot be compared with ==
questions.explanation: The == operator compares references, not contents. A literal comes from the string pool, while new String() always allocates a fresh object on the heap. Calling equals() would give true; == gives false.

questions.question: Two Integer variables are boxed from 127 and two more from 128. Comparing each pair with ==, what do you get?
options: true for the 127 pair and false for the 128 pair
true for both pairs
false for both pairs
false for the 127 pair and true for the 128 pair
questions.explanation: Autoboxing routes through Integer.valueOf(), which caches instances from -128 to 127. Both 127 boxes are therefore the same object, while each 128 allocates a new object. Always use equals() to compare boxed values.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the eight Java primitive types?
options: String
char
boolean
byte
questions.explanation: The eight primitives are byte, short, int, long, float, double, char and boolean. String is a class in java.lang; it just gets special treatment from the compiler that makes it feel built in.

questions.question: What does printing the expression 7 / 2 display in Java?
questions.explanation: Both operands are int, so Java performs integer division and truncates toward zero. The fractional part is discarded, not rounded. Making one operand a double gives 3.5.

questions.question: A List field is declared final and initialised with a new ArrayList. Which statement is true?
options: You can add and remove elements, but cannot reassign the variable to another list
The list becomes immutable, so add() throws UnsupportedOperationException
Both reassignment and mutation are blocked by the compiler
final has no effect on reference variables, only on primitives
questions.explanation: final freezes the reference, not the object it points at. Reassigning the variable is a compile error, but adding to the list works fine. For genuine immutability you need List.copyOf() or Collections.unmodifiableList().

questions.question: When does a static initializer block run?
options: Once, when the class is first loaded and initialized, before main() or any instance exists
Every time an object of the class is constructed, just before the constructor body
Only when a static method on the class is explicitly called
After main() finishes, as part of class unloading
questions.explanation: Static blocks belong to the class, not to instances. The JVM runs them exactly once during class initialization, in source order. Instance initializer blocks, written without the static keyword, are the ones that run per construction.

questions.question: A new int array and a new String array are both allocated with length 3. What do their first elements hold?
options: 0 and null
null and null
0 and an empty string
Nothing, both throw until you assign elements
questions.explanation: Array elements are fields of the array object, so they take type defaults: 0 for int and null for any reference type. Calling a method on the String element would throw NullPointerException, because allocating the array does not allocate the Strings inside it.

questions.question: Why is concatenating Strings with the + operator inside a long loop discouraged?
options: String is immutable, so each concatenation allocates a new object and copies every existing character
The string pool overflows and throws OutOfMemoryError after about 1000 iterations
String concatenation is not thread safe inside loops
The compiler rejects the + operator on String inside a for loop
questions.explanation: Every concatenation produces a brand new object and copies all existing characters, making the loop quadratic in the total length. StringBuilder mutates one internal buffer instead, which is why it is the right tool for loop accumulation.

questions.question: A char literal holding the letter a is added to the int 1. What is the type and value of that expression?
options: int, with the value 98
char, with the value b
String, with the value a1
It does not compile, because char and int cannot be added
questions.explanation: char is a 16-bit integral type, so binary numeric promotion widens it to int: the letter a is 97, giving 98. Printing the expression shows 98, not b. An explicit char cast is needed to get the letter back.

questions.question: Which signature will the JVM accept as an application entry point?
options: public static void main(String... args)
public void main(String[] args)
static void main(String[] args)
public static int main(String[] args)
questions.explanation: The entry point must be public, static, return void and take a single String array. Varargs compiles down to String[], so it qualifies. Dropping public, dropping static or returning int all make the JVM fail to find main.

questions.question: From which Java version can a switch statement operate on a String?
options: Java 7
Java 5
Java 8
Strings are still not permitted in switch
questions.explanation: Java 7 added String in switch, compiled as a hashCode() lookup followed by equals() checks. Java 5 had earlier added enums in switch, and Java 14 added switch expressions with the arrow form.

questions.question: A method reassigns its object parameter to a brand new object. What does the caller observe afterwards?
options: Nothing changes for the caller, because Java passes the reference by value
The caller variable now points at the new object
A compile error, because parameters are implicitly final
The original object is garbage collected immediately
questions.explanation: Java is strictly pass-by-value; for objects the value copied is the reference itself. Mutating the object through the parameter IS visible to the caller, but reassigning the parameter only repoints the local copy.

questions.question: Why does Java forbid a class from extending more than one class?
options: To avoid the diamond problem, where two parents supply conflicting implementations of the same method
Because the JVM can only store one superclass pointer per object header
Because it would make every method call slower at runtime
It is an arbitrary restriction that interfaces later removed entirely
questions.explanation: With two superclasses defining the same method, the compiler cannot tell which implementation to inherit. Interfaces sidestep this because, before default methods, they carried no implementation at all, and Java 8 requires you to resolve any default-method clash explicitly.

questions.question: When is an overloaded method resolved, compared with an overridden one?
options: Overloading is resolved at compile time from the declared types; overriding is dispatched at runtime from the actual object
Both are resolved at compile time from the declared types
Both are dispatched at runtime from the actual object
Overloading is resolved at runtime; overriding is resolved at compile time
questions.explanation: Overload selection is static: the compiler picks a signature using the reference types it can see. Overriding is dynamic dispatch: the JVM looks at the object actually on the heap. This is why passing null to overloaded methods can be ambiguous at compile time.

questions.question: What happens when a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as a static method in its parent?
options: The parent method is hidden, not overridden, and which one runs depends on the reference type
It is a normal override and dynamic dispatch applies
The code fails to compile, because static methods cannot be redeclared
The parent method is removed from the subclass entirely
questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the class, so there is no dynamic dispatch. This is method hiding: a Parent-typed reference calls the parent version even when it points at a Child instance. Marking such a method with the override annotation is a compile error.

questions.question: Can an abstract class declare a constructor?
options: Yes, and it runs via super() when a concrete subclass is instantiated
No, because an abstract class can never be instantiated
Yes, but it is silently ignored at runtime
Only if the class also declares at least one abstract method
questions.explanation: Abstract classes hold state, and that state needs initialising. You cannot call new on the abstract type directly, but the constructor still runs as part of building a concrete subclass instance, which is exactly why it is allowed.

questions.question: Since Java 8 interfaces can carry default methods. What still separates an abstract class from an interface?
options: An abstract class can hold mutable instance state and constructors; an interface cannot
Nothing, they became functionally identical in Java 8
Only an abstract class may declare concrete methods
A class can implement only one interface but extend many abstract classes
questions.explanation: Interface fields are implicitly public, static and final, so an interface cannot carry per-instance state, and it has no constructor. An abstract class can do both, which is why it stays the right choice when subclasses share data rather than just behaviour.

questions.question: A parent declares a private method. The child declares a method with the identical name and signature. What is the relationship?
options: None, they are unrelated methods, because a private method is not visible to subclasses
The child overrides the parent method as usual
The code fails to compile because of the name clash
The child method is implicitly made private too
questions.explanation: Overriding requires the parent method to be visible to the subclass. A private method is not inherited at all, so the child simply declares a brand new method that happens to share a name.

questions.question: An overriding method returns a subtype of the type the parent method returned. Is that legal?
options: Yes, this is a covariant return type and has been allowed since Java 5
No, an override must match the parent return type exactly
Only if the parent method is abstract
Only for primitive return types
questions.explanation: Java 5 relaxed the rule so an override may narrow the return type. Any caller holding the parent type still gets something assignable to what it expected, so type safety is preserved. Parameter types, by contrast, must still match exactly.

questions.question: What does encapsulation actually buy you beyond making fields private?
options: The class can change its internal representation without breaking callers, and can enforce invariants on every change
It makes the object immutable
It makes field access faster because the JVM can inline private fields
It is required for a class to be serializable
questions.explanation: Private fields plus accessors give you a seam. You can swap the internal data structure, add validation, or start logging, all without touching a single caller. Getters and setters that blindly expose every field give up most of that benefit.

questions.question: A constructor body does not begin with this() or super(). What does the compiler do?
options: It inserts a call to the no-argument super() constructor as the first statement
It skips the parent constructor entirely
It reports an error demanding an explicit call
It calls every parent constructor in declaration order
questions.explanation: Java guarantees the parent is initialised before the child body runs, so it inserts super() for you. If the parent has no accessible no-argument constructor, that inserted call fails to compile, which is the usual cause of the confusing error about a missing super constructor.

questions.question: What distinguishes a checked exception from an unchecked one?
options: A checked exception must be caught or declared with throws; unchecked ones extend RuntimeException and need neither
A checked exception is detected by the JVM, an unchecked one by the compiler
Checked exceptions can be recovered from, unchecked ones always terminate the program
Unchecked exceptions cannot be caught at all
questions.explanation: The split is purely a compile-time contract. Anything extending Exception but not RuntimeException is checked, so the compiler forces you to handle or declare it. RuntimeException and Error sit outside that rule.

questions.question: Which situation stops a finally block from running?
options: A call to System.exit() inside the try block
An exception thrown inside the try block
A return statement inside the try block
A break statement that leaves the try block
questions.explanation: return, break and thrown exceptions all still run finally on the way out. System.exit() halts the JVM immediately, so finally never executes. A JVM crash or a killed thread has the same effect.

questions.question: A method returns a value from its try block, and the finally block also returns a different value. What does the caller receive?
options: The value returned by finally, because it overwrites the pending return
The value returned by try, because it was evaluated first
A compile error, since two returns conflict
Both values, wrapped in an array
questions.explanation: A return inside finally discards the pending return value, and it will also swallow an in-flight exception. That silent loss is why most style guides ban returning from finally outright.

questions.question: You write catch(Exception e) before catch(IOException e) in the same try. What happens?
options: A compile error, because IOException is already covered by the earlier, broader catch
It compiles, and IOException is routed to the second block
It compiles, but the second block is silently dead code
It compiles and both blocks run for an IOException
questions.explanation: Catch clauses are tested top to bottom, so a broader type first makes any narrower type below it unreachable. The compiler rejects this outright. Always order catch blocks from most specific to most general.

questions.question: Two resources are opened in a single try-with-resources statement. In what order are they closed?
options: Reverse of declaration order, so the last opened closes first
Declaration order, so the first opened closes first
Unspecified, the JVM may choose either
Only the first resource is closed automatically
questions.explanation: Resources close in reverse order, mirroring how nested try-finally blocks would unwind. This matters when a later resource wraps an earlier one, such as a BufferedReader over a FileReader.

questions.question: Why should application code normally avoid catching Error?
options: Error signals a serious JVM-level failure such as OutOfMemoryError that the application usually cannot recover from
Error cannot be caught, so the catch block never compiles
Catching Error is a compile error unless the method declares it
Error and Exception are interchangeable, so catching either is equivalent
questions.explanation: Throwable splits into Exception, which your code is expected to handle, and Error, which reports conditions like a stack overflow or exhausted heap. Catching Error usually just hides a fatal problem and leaves the JVM in an unreliable state.

questions.question: What is the difference between calling start() and calling run() on a Thread?
options: start() asks the JVM for a new thread of execution; run() is an ordinary method call on the current thread
They are equivalent, start() is just the conventional name
run() creates the thread and start() begins it, so both are required
start() is asynchronous and run() blocks until the thread finishes
questions.explanation: Calling run() directly executes the body on whichever thread called it, so nothing runs concurrently. Only start() registers a new thread with the scheduler, which then invokes run() for you.

questions.question: What happens if start() is called twice on the same Thread object?
options: The second call throws IllegalThreadStateException
The thread restarts from the beginning of run()
A second thread is created that shares the same run() body
The second call is silently ignored
questions.explanation: A Thread object is single use. Once it has been started it can never return to the NEW state, so a second start() is rejected. To run the same task again, submit it to an executor or build a fresh Thread.

questions.question: What does declaring a field volatile guarantee?
options: Visibility, so a write is seen by other threads, but not atomicity of compound operations
Both visibility and atomicity, making increments thread safe
That only one thread may access the field at a time
That the field is stored in CPU registers for speed
questions.explanation: volatile stops the value being cached per thread and forbids certain reorderings, so a write becomes visible. It does nothing for read-modify-write sequences: count++ is still three operations and can still lose updates. Use AtomicInteger or a lock for that.

questions.question: A class has one synchronized instance method and one synchronized static method. Can two threads run them at the same time?
options: Yes, because they lock different monitors: the instance versus the class object
No, synchronized always serialises every method on the class
No, because static methods implicitly lock the instance too
Only if the object is declared volatile
questions.explanation: A synchronized instance method locks this, while a synchronized static method locks the Class object. They are independent monitors, so the two calls do not exclude each other. Mixing the two is a common source of races.

questions.question: Calling wait() on an object outside a synchronized block produces what?
options: IllegalMonitorStateException at runtime
A compile error
It works, but the thread never wakes up
A deadlock
questions.explanation: wait(), notify() and notifyAll() require the calling thread to already own the monitor, since wait() has to release it atomically. The compiler cannot verify that, so the check happens at runtime.

questions.question: How do Thread.sleep() and Object.wait() differ with respect to locks?
options: sleep() keeps every lock the thread holds; wait() releases the monitor it was called on
Both release all held locks
Both keep all held locks
wait() keeps its lock while sleep() releases them
questions.explanation: sleep() is a timing operation and knows nothing about monitors, so sleeping inside a synchronized block blocks everyone else for the whole duration. wait() exists precisely to release the monitor so another thread can make progress and notify.

questions.question: Two threads each hold one lock and wait for the other. Which change reliably prevents this deadlock?
options: Make every thread acquire the locks in the same global order
Make both locks volatile
Increase the thread pool size so more threads are available
Replace synchronized with synchronized static methods
questions.explanation: Deadlock needs a circular wait, and a consistent global lock ordering makes a cycle impossible. Timeouts via tryLock() are the other common defence. Adding threads or changing lock visibility does nothing to break the cycle.

questions.question: Why is ArrayList usually the better default than LinkedList, even for lists you insert into often?
options: ArrayList gives O(1) random access and far better cache locality; LinkedList pays a pointer chase and an object header per element
LinkedList cannot grow beyond its initial capacity
ArrayList inserts in the middle in O(1) while LinkedList needs O(n)
LinkedList is not thread safe but ArrayList is
questions.explanation: LinkedList only wins when you insert or remove at a position you already hold an iterator for. Its nodes are scattered across the heap, so traversal misses cache constantly, and each node carries its own header plus two references.

questions.question: You use a custom class as a HashMap key and override equals() but not hashCode(). What goes wrong?
options: Two equal keys can land in different buckets, so a lookup with an equal key fails to find the entry
The map throws IllegalStateException on the first put
Nothing, hashCode() is only used by HashSet
The code fails to compile, because equals and hashCode must be overridden together
questions.explanation: HashMap picks a bucket from hashCode() and only then compares with equals(). The inherited identity hashCode differs per object, so an equal-but-distinct key usually probes the wrong bucket and reports a miss. The contract requires equal objects to share a hash code.

questions.question: What did Java 8 change about how HashMap handles a bucket with many colliding entries?
options: A long collision chain converts into a balanced tree, improving worst case lookup from O(n) to O(log n)
Colliding entries are rehashed into a second backing array
The map throws an exception once a bucket exceeds eight entries
Collisions were eliminated entirely by a new hash function
questions.explanation: Once a bucket holds enough entries and the table is large enough, the linked chain becomes a red-black tree. This caps the damage from hash-collision attacks and from poor hashCode implementations.

questions.question: How is HashSet implemented internally?
options: It wraps a HashMap, storing each element as a key mapped to one shared dummy value
It uses a sorted array with binary search
It uses a linked list with a uniqueness check on every add
It is a primitive JVM structure with no Java-level backing collection
questions.explanation: HashSet delegates almost everything to a private HashMap, which is why it inherits the same hashCode and equals requirements and the same average O(1) behaviour. LinkedHashSet and TreeSet wrap LinkedHashMap and TreeMap the same way.

questions.question: Removing an element by calling list.remove() inside an enhanced for loop over that list usually throws what?
options: ConcurrentModificationException, because the iterator detects structural modification
IndexOutOfBoundsException, because the list shrank
UnsupportedOperationException, because lists are immutable while iterating
Nothing, this is the standard way to remove elements
questions.explanation: The iterator records a modification count and checks it on each step; changing the list behind its back trips the fail-fast guard. Use iterator.remove(), removeIf(), or collect the survivors into a new list.

questions.question: When should you reach for Comparator rather than Comparable?
options: When you need several orderings, or cannot modify the class being sorted
When the collection holds primitives rather than objects
When sorting must be stable
When the list has more than a thousand elements
questions.explanation: Comparable bakes one natural ordering into the class itself, so a type can have only one. Comparator lives outside the class, letting you sort the same type by name, then by date, and letting you order classes you do not own.

questions.question: What is the practical difference between Vector and ArrayList?
options: Vector synchronizes every method, which makes it slower and still does not make compound operations safe
Vector cannot be resized after construction
ArrayList is a legacy class that Vector replaced
Vector stores primitives while ArrayList stores objects
questions.explanation: Vector locks on each individual call, so check-then-act sequences still race, and the locking costs you throughput even in single-threaded code. For genuinely concurrent use, prefer CopyOnWriteArrayList or an explicit lock.

questions.question: What happens when you call add() on a list created by List.of()?
options: It throws UnsupportedOperationException, because the list is immutable
The element is appended normally
It returns false and leaves the list unchanged
It fails to compile, because List.of() returns a different interface
questions.explanation: The factory methods added in Java 9 return genuinely immutable lists that reject every mutating operation, and they also reject null elements. Arrays.asList() is different again: fixed size, but set() still works.

questions.question: How many times does the container call init() and service() on a servlet?
options: init() once when the servlet is first loaded; service() once per request
Both once per request
Both once, when the application starts
init() once per request; service() once per session
questions.explanation: The container creates a single servlet instance, calls init() once to set it up, then dispatches every incoming request through service(). destroy() runs once at shutdown. This is why init() is the place for expensive one-time setup.

questions.question: Why are instance fields on a servlet dangerous?
options: One servlet instance serves all concurrent requests, so instance fields are shared mutable state across threads
The container serialises instance fields to disk between requests
Instance fields are reset to null before every request
They are not dangerous, the container creates one servlet per request
questions.explanation: The single-instance, multi-thread model means two users can be inside service() at the same time. Anything stored in an instance field is shared between them. Keep per-request state in local variables or in the request object.

questions.question: What is the key difference between RequestDispatcher.forward() and response.sendRedirect()?
options: forward() happens server side and keeps the same request; sendRedirect() tells the browser to make a second request
forward() is faster because it skips the container
sendRedirect() preserves request attributes while forward() discards them
They are identical apart from the URL shown in the address bar
questions.explanation: A forward is invisible to the client: the URL does not change and request attributes survive. A redirect sends a 302 and the browser issues a fresh request, so attributes are lost and the URL updates, which is what you want after a POST.

questions.question: Which statement about doGet and doPost is accurate?
options: GET parameters ride in the query string and the request may be cached or bookmarked; POST sends them in the body
POST can carry parameters but GET cannot
GET is encrypted while POST is plain text
Only doPost can return HTML
questions.explanation: Neither method is encrypted, that is what TLS is for. The real differences are where parameters travel, that GET is expected to be safe and idempotent, and that GET responses can be cached and bookmarked.

questions.question: HttpSession needs to identify a returning browser. What does the container use by default?
options: A JSESSIONID cookie, falling back to URL rewriting when cookies are disabled
The client IP address
A hidden form field injected into every page
The browser user-agent string
questions.explanation: HTTP is stateless, so the session id has to travel with each request. Cookies are the default carrier; encodeURL() appends the id to links when cookies are unavailable. IP addresses are unusable because proxies and NAT share them.

questions.question: What separates ServletConfig from ServletContext?
options: ServletConfig holds parameters for one servlet; ServletContext is shared across the whole web application
ServletConfig is read-only while ServletContext is writable
ServletContext exists only during a single request
They are two names for the same object
questions.explanation: Each servlet gets its own ServletConfig with its own init parameters. There is exactly one ServletContext per application, which is why it is the place for application-wide attributes, and why writing to it needs care under concurrency.

questions.question: What happens to a JSP page the first time it is requested?
options: The container translates it into servlet source, compiles it, and then runs it like any other servlet
It is interpreted line by line on every request
It is sent to the browser, which renders the JSP tags
It is converted to static HTML and cached permanently
questions.explanation: JSP is a servlet-authoring convenience. The container generates a servlet whose service method writes your markup, compiles it once, then reuses it. That translation step is why the first hit to a JSP is noticeably slower.

questions.question: What is a servlet Filter designed for?
options: Intercepting requests and responses to apply cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, logging or compression
Filtering invalid characters out of form parameters only
Choosing which servlet handles a URL pattern
Rejecting requests from unknown IP addresses, and nothing else
questions.explanation: Filters form a chain around the target servlet, so they can inspect or wrap both the request on the way in and the response on the way out. That makes them the natural home for concerns that would otherwise be duplicated in every servlet.

questions.question: Where do a local reference variable and the object it points at actually live?
options: The reference sits in the thread stack frame; the object itself is on the shared heap
Both live on the stack for speed
Both live on the heap, the stack only holds primitives
The reference is on the heap and the object is in the method area
questions.explanation: Each thread owns a private stack holding frames of locals, which is why locals are inherently thread safe. Objects are allocated on the heap and shared, which is exactly why they need synchronisation.

questions.question: Which JVM memory area is private to each thread?
options: The stack and the program counter register
The heap
The method area
The string pool
questions.explanation: Every thread gets its own stack, PC register and native method stack. The heap and the method area (metaspace) are shared, which is the root of every visibility and race problem in Java.

questions.question: What replaced PermGen in Java 8, and where does it live?
options: Metaspace, which is allocated in native memory rather than the Java heap
The old generation, which absorbed all class metadata
The code cache, which now stores class definitions
Nothing, PermGen is still used and simply resized
questions.explanation: Class metadata moved out of the fixed-size PermGen into native memory, so it grows as needed and the classic PermGen OutOfMemoryError largely disappeared. It can still be capped with MaxMetaspaceSize.

questions.question: What assumption underpins generational garbage collection?
options: Most objects die young, so collecting a small young generation frequently reclaims most garbage cheaply
Objects are collected in the order they were allocated
Large objects are collected before small ones
Every object survives at least one collection cycle
questions.explanation: The weak generational hypothesis says the vast majority of allocations become unreachable almost immediately. Collecting Eden often, and promoting only the survivors, keeps the common case fast and leaves the expensive old-generation work rare.

questions.question: Java has a garbage collector, so how can an application still leak memory?
options: Objects stay reachable from a long-lived structure such as a static collection or cache, so the collector may not reclaim them
The collector only runs when the heap is completely full
Leaks are impossible in Java by design
Only native code called through JNI can leak
questions.explanation: The collector reclaims unreachable objects, not unused ones. A static map that is only ever added to, an unremoved listener, or a ThreadLocal never cleared, all keep objects reachable forever. That is a leak in every practical sense.

questions.question: What distinguishes OutOfMemoryError from StackOverflowError?
options: OutOfMemoryError means the heap or metaspace is exhausted; StackOverflowError means one thread exceeded its stack depth, usually via unbounded recursion
They are two names for the same condition
StackOverflowError comes from the heap and OutOfMemoryError from the stack
OutOfMemoryError is a checked exception while StackOverflowError is not
questions.explanation: They exhaust different regions. A deep or infinite recursion blows the per-thread stack; retaining too many live objects, or leaking them, exhausts the heap. Both extend Error, so neither is checked.

questions.question: What does the JIT compiler do that the interpreter does not?
options: It compiles frequently executed bytecode into native machine code at runtime, using observed profile data to optimise
It compiles source files into bytecode before execution
It removes unused classes from the heap
It verifies bytecode for security violations
questions.explanation: The JVM starts interpreting, watches which methods and loops run hot, then compiles those to native code. Because it optimises against real runtime behaviour it can inline and speculate in ways an ahead-of-time compiler cannot, which is why long-running Java gets faster over time.

questions.question: Your application hangs with low CPU usage. Which diagnostic is most useful first?
options: A thread dump, to see what every thread is blocked on and detect a deadlock
A heap dump, to list the largest objects
A GC log, to measure pause times
A JIT compilation log
questions.explanation: Low CPU with no progress points at blocking, not allocation. A thread dump shows each thread state and the monitors it holds or waits for, and the JVM will explicitly report a detected deadlock. Heap dumps are the tool for memory growth instead.

questions.question: Where do a local reference variable and the object it points at actually live?
options: The reference sits in the thread stack frame; the object itself is on the shared heap
Both live on the stack for speed
Both live on the heap, the stack only holds primitives
The reference is on the heap and the object is in the method area
questions.explanation: Each thread owns a private stack holding frames of locals, which is why locals are inherently thread safe. Objects are allocated on the heap and shared, which is exactly why they need synchronisation.

The heap
The method area
The string pool

questions.question: Which is the most robust way to implement a Singleton in Java?
options: A single-element enum, which the JVM guarantees against reflection and serialization attacks
A static field initialised lazily with a plain null check
A synchronized getInstance() that allocates on first call
A public static final field of an ordinary class
questions.explanation: The enum form is initialised once by the class loader, and the language forbids reflective instantiation and handles serialization correctly. A plain lazy null check is not thread safe, and even double-checked locking needs volatile to be correct.

questions.question: What separates the Factory Method pattern from Abstract Factory?
options: Factory Method defers creation of one product to a subclass; Abstract Factory creates whole families of related products
Abstract Factory is simply the interface version of Factory Method
Factory Method can only create immutable objects
Abstract Factory is limited to a single product type
questions.explanation: Factory Method is one overridable creation hook. Abstract Factory groups several such hooks behind one interface so an entire family stays consistent, which is how UI toolkits keep every widget on the same theme.

questions.question: Which problem does the Builder pattern primarily solve?
options: Constructing an object with many optional parameters without a combinatorial explosion of constructors
Guaranteeing only one instance of a class exists
Letting incompatible interfaces work together
Adding behaviour to an object at runtime
questions.explanation: Builder replaces the telescoping-constructor anti-pattern with readable, named steps and can validate the whole object in build(). It also makes immutable objects with many fields practical to construct.

questions.question: Both Adapter and Decorator wrap another object. What is the difference in intent?
options: Adapter changes an interface to one the client expects; Decorator keeps the interface and adds behaviour
Adapter adds behaviour while Decorator changes the interface
Adapter works on classes and Decorator only on interfaces
They are the same pattern under two names
questions.explanation: Structure alone does not identify a pattern, intent does. Adapter exists to translate a mismatched interface. Decorator deliberately preserves the interface so wrappers can stack, which is how the java.io streams compose.

questions.question: When is Strategy the right pattern?
options: When several interchangeable algorithms exist and the choice should be made at runtime without conditionals scattered through the code
When an object must notify many dependants of state changes
When object creation must be centralised
When you need to add responsibilities to an object dynamically
questions.explanation: Strategy turns a growing if-else or switch over behaviour into a set of small classes behind one interface, chosen by injection. In modern Java a strategy is often just a lambda, since the interface is usually functional.

questions.question: Which JDK feature is the clearest real-world example of the Observer pattern?
options: Listener registration in Swing and JavaFX, where components notify registered handlers of events
The java.io decorator stream hierarchy
The Collections.unmodifiableList wrapper
The Runtime.getRuntime() accessor
questions.explanation: Event listeners are Observer in its canonical form: a subject keeps a list of registered observers and pushes updates to all of them. The original java.util.Observer was deprecated in Java 9 for being too limited.

questions.question: What does a Proxy add that a plain reference does not?
options: A stand-in that controls access, enabling lazy loading, security checks, caching or remote invocation
A guarantee that only one instance exists
The ability to convert between incompatible interfaces
A snapshot of the object state for undo support
questions.explanation: Proxy shares the subject interface but interposes logic around the real object. Hibernate lazy loading and Spring AOP both work this way, which is why a lazily loaded entity can throw once its session is closed.

questions.question: How does Template Method structure an algorithm?
options: A base class fixes the overall sequence in a final method and leaves specific steps for subclasses to override
Each step is a separate object chosen at runtime
The algorithm is chosen by a factory at construction time
Steps are chained so each decides whether to pass the request on
questions.explanation: The skeleton lives in one place and is usually final so subclasses cannot reorder it; only the designated hook methods vary. Strategy solves a similar problem with composition instead of inheritance, which is generally more flexible.
